title: Circular and Square Seating
summary: Seating around a round table and around a square or rectangular one: which way is left when you face the centre, how facing outward reverses it, counting positions and opposite seats, and where people sit at corners and mid-sides.
learningObjectives: State which circular direction is a person's left when they face the centre.
Reverse left and right for a person who faces outward.
Count 'third to the left' and find the opposite seat around a circle.
Lay out a square table with people at corners and mid-sides.

blocks.title: Round tables and square tables
blocks.markdown:
Two table shapes carry most of these puzzles:

- **Round table:** people sit evenly around a circle. All may face the centre, all may face outward, or the puzzle may mix the two.
- **Square or rectangular table:** people sit at the corners and at the middle of each side. Corner people and mid-side people often face different ways.

As with a row, the clues fix exactly one seating. The extra care a circle needs is over left and right, because those depend on which way each person faces.

blocks.title: Facing outward reverses left and right
blocks.markdown:
Turn the same person around to face **outward** and their left and right swap:

- their **left** is now the next seat anticlockwise, seat number minus one;
- their **right** is the next seat clockwise, seat number plus one.

In a mixed puzzle you must apply the rule **per person**, checking which way that particular person faces before you place a neighbour. A clue such as "S is immediately to the left of the outward-facing T" places S one seat anticlockwise of T, not clockwise.

A short check: if X and Y sit next to each other but face opposite ways, then X is on Y's left exactly when Y is also on X's left.

blocks.title: Counting positions and opposite seats
blocks.markdown:
- To move "k to the left" of someone, take k single steps in their left direction, wrapping past the highest seat number back to 1.
- **Between** two people means the shorter arc unless the puzzle says "counting clockwise" or names a side.
- On a circle with an **even** number of seats, the seat **directly opposite** seat n is the one halfway round: for eight seats, opposite seat n is seat n plus four (wrapping). For ten seats it is n plus five.
- An odd circle has no exactly-opposite seat; "opposite" there means the pair of seats closest to halfway.

blocks.title: Square and rectangular tables
blocks.markdown:
Lay the eight seats out clockwise as corner, mid-side, corner, mid-side, and so on. Keep two facts straight from the clue text:

- **Which seats face which way.** A common setup has the four corner people facing the centre and the four mid-side people facing outward, but always read it from the puzzle.
- **Opposite seats.** A corner is opposite the corner two places round; a mid-side seat is opposite the mid-side seat two places round.

Once facings are marked, the left and right rules are exactly those for a circle: plus one clockwise for a centre-facer's left, minus one for an outward-facer's left.

blocks.title: Worked example: mixed circle
blocks.markdown:
Eight people A to H sit around a circular table. All face the centre except D and G, who face outward. Seats are numbered 1 to 8 clockwise.

- (1) A sits second to the right of C.
- (2) B sits between A and C.
- (3) D is an immediate neighbour of C.
- (4) E sits immediately to the right of D.
- (5) G sits directly opposite C.
- (6) F sits between E and G.
- (7) H is an immediate neighbour of both A and G.

**Solve.** Fix C, say at seat 3. By (1), A is two seats to C's right; C faces the centre, so right is anticlockwise, putting A at seat 1. By (2), B is the single seat between them, seat 2. By (3), D neighbours C on the other side, seat 4. D faces **outward**, so by (4) D's right is clockwise and E is at seat 5. By (5), G is opposite C, seat 7. By (6), F is the seat between E and G, seat 6. By (7), the last seat, 8, sits between A and G and is H.

**Clockwise order from seat 1: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Using one left-right rule for the whole table** when some people face outward. The rule is per person.
- **Forgetting to wrap** the count past the highest seat number.
- **Taking the long arc** for "between" when the shorter arc was meant.
- **Reading "opposite" on an odd circle** as an exact seat; there isn't one.
- **Mixing corner and mid-side seats** on a square table, or losing track of which set faces which way.
- **Not re-checking every clue** against the finished circle, including the facing of each person.

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- Number seats clockwise. Facing the centre: left is plus one (clockwise), right is minus one. Facing outward: the reverse.
- Apply the left-right rule separately for each person, after checking which way they face.
- "k to the left" is k single steps, wrapping past the last seat. "Between" is the shorter arc unless a side is named.
- On an even circle, opposite seat n is n plus half the seats. An odd circle has no exact opposite.
- On a square table, set corners and mid-sides, mark facings, then use the circle rules.

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
Eight people P to W sit around a square table. P, R, T, V are at the four corners and face the centre; Q, S, U, W are at the middle of the four sides and face outward. Seats are numbered 1 to 8 clockwise as corner, mid-side, corner, mid-side, and so on. "Nth to the left or right of X" means N seats from X in X's own left or right direction.

- (1) R sits second to the left of P.
- (2) Q sits between P and R.
- (3) T sits directly opposite P.
- (4) S sits immediately to the right of T.
- (5) V sits directly opposite R.
- (6) U sits immediately to the right of V.
- (7) W sits between V and P.

Fix the arrangement, then answer, each with a one-line reason:

1. Who sits immediately to the right of P?
2. Who sits between R and T?
3. How is U placed with respect to T?
4. Who sits second to the left of W?
5. Which one of Q, S, U, V sits at a corner?

flashcards.front: Seats numbered clockwise. For a person facing the centre, which seat is on their left?
flashcards.back: The next seat clockwise, that is seat number plus one. Their right is the next seat anticlockwise, seat number minus one.
flashcards.explanation: Picture the six-o'clock seat facing in: the left hand points the clockwise way.

flashcards.front: How do left and right change for a person facing outward?
flashcards.back: They swap. Left becomes the next seat anticlockwise (minus one); right becomes the next seat clockwise (plus one).
flashcards.explanation: Turning to face out mirrors the person's sense of left and right.

flashcards.front: In a mixed circle, how many times do you decide the left-right rule?
flashcards.back: Once per person. Check which way that person faces before placing anyone to their left or right.
flashcards.explanation: One rule for the whole table is the classic mixed-circle mistake.

flashcards.front: On a table with 8 seats, which seat is directly opposite seat n?
flashcards.back: Seat n plus 4, wrapping past 8 back to 1. On a 10-seat circle it is n plus 5. An odd circle has no exact opposite.
flashcards.explanation: Opposite is always half the seats around.

flashcards.front: 'C sits between A and B' around a circle — which arc?
flashcards.back: The shorter arc, unless the puzzle says 'counting clockwise' or names a side.
flashcards.explanation: Assuming the long arc creates room for a wrong placement.

flashcards.front: How do you lay out a square table for eight people?
flashcards.back: Seats clockwise as corner, mid-side, corner, mid-side, and so on. Mark which set faces the centre and which faces outward, then use the circle left-right rules.
flashcards.explanation: Opposite corner is two places round; opposite mid-side is two places round.

flashcards.front: How do you count 'third to the left' around a circle?
flashcards.back: Three single steps in that person's left direction, wrapping past the highest seat number back to seat 1.
flashcards.explanation: Forgetting the wrap lands you one seat short or on no seat at all.
